Glossary

# a priori / a posteriori

from what is prior / from what is subsequent

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / a priori / a posteriori

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Certainty](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/certainty) · [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason) · [Experience](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/experience) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Science](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/science) · [Limits](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/limits)

## What the term does

The distinction between knowledge that can be established without recourse to experience and knowledge that depends on it. In Kant the pair becomes central and is separated from the analytic–synthetic distinction: an a priori judgement is one whose necessity and strict universality cannot be derived from experience, and Kant's question in the Critique of Pure Reason is how such judgements are possible at all. That mathematics and the principle of causation seem to be of this kind, yet deliver information about the world, is the problem the whole critical project is built to answer.

## The reading the sources do not support

Equated with 'analytic' (true by meaning) or with 'innate'. Both equations are later and are exactly what Kant is at pains to keep apart: 7 + 5 = 12 is for him a priori and synthetic, and he argues no innate idea is required.
